beats.text: You just admitted you messed up. And now you can't stop cringing.
But here's what everyone else saw.
In seven studies, people pictured moments of vulnerability. Admitting a mistake. Confessing their love. Improvising a song in front of a jury.
When it was them, it looked more like weakness.
When it was someone else, it looked more like courage.
Researchers call it the beautiful mess effect.
Up close, you see every messy detail. From the outside, people see the whole picture.
And people who are kinder to themselves show a smaller gap.
So that moment you're cringing about? To them, it might have looked brave.

sources: Bruk, Scholl & Bless (2018). Beautiful mess effect: Self-other differences in evaluation of showing vulnerability. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. Seven studies; scenarios incl. confessing romantic love, admitting a mistake; one study expecting to improvise a song before a jury. Own vulnerability rated more negatively (more weakness, less courage) than others'. Explanation: construal level (concrete self vs abstract other).

Bruk, Scholl & Bless (2022). You and I both: Self-compassion reduces self-other differences in evaluation of showing vulnerability. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin. Three studies: self-compassion (not self-esteem/neuroticism) associated with a smaller self-other gap.
BPS Research Digest on the beautiful mess effect.
